Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Threat of shock increases excitability and connectivity of the intraparietal sulcus" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by David Van Essen (Senior editor), a Reviewing editor, and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

We thank the authors for their careful consideration of the comments of all three reviewers, and for the extra analyses that have been undertaken. The paper is much improved as a result of these changes and is now close to publication. However, a few points remain to be addressed.

1) I consider the conjunction map, provided in the response to reviewers, to be critical to the paper and I would very much like to see this in the main paper, perhaps added to Figure 7.

2) Its rather a shame that the MEG connectivity analysis didn't work, but nevertheless I thank the authors for attempting it. I wonder however if some extra clarification could be given: What frequency band was connectivity computed in (sincere apologies if I missed it)? I assume α? I'm also unsure as to what is meant by "we then computed the Hilbert transform using a 500 ms sliding window"? The Hilbert transform shouldn't need a sliding window – when undertaking this analysis we usually compute the HT over all time? Please clarify why this was done. Could the authors please show the MEG adjacency matrices for the safe and thread blocks independently, as well as the difference? This would allow the reader to confirm that the two separate matrices look sensible (one expects large occipital connectivity in the α band, see e.g. Hunt et al., 2016). Finally, given the strong finding of MEG connectivity in the β band, I would like to see the connectivity analysis attempted in this band. I of course read the authors argument that "one might expect a high degree of stationarity in coherence of the β oscillations across time" but I disagree, specifically because multiple papers (e.g. O'Neill et al., 2015; O'Neill et al., 2016; Baker et al., 2014) show that, in fact, β band functional connectivity is highly dynamic.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Threat of shock increases excitability and connectivity of the intraparietal sulcus" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by David Van Essen (Senior editor) and the Reviewing editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

I thank the authors for going to such lengths on the MEG connectivity analysis. However, something has clearly gone wrong here in the analysis.

By my assessment of the adjacency matrices presented, the case for the α and β bands look virtually identical. However this should not be the case (again see Hunt et al, 2016). It is quite hard for me to judge the spatial signature of connectivity as, unfortunately, in the pdf version the figure quality is too low resolution to read the region names on the axes. However, these matrices do not look correct to me and I would urge the authors to find out why.

In their response, the authors have suggested that they use blocks of only 2 seconds of envelope data. However they also apply downsampling prior to connectivity estimation. This to me seems silly – why apply the downsampling if you have such short blocks. It is well established that connectivity works without the downsampling so perhaps removing that step might improve the adjacency matrices. I also don't understand why such short data setments were used when in fact the blocks are quite long. Why not just try using the whole block?

I remain enthusiastic about this article, but I maintain that the MEG connectivity analysis has not yet been properly carried out. I would want to see this estimated reliably (or a concrete argument on why it cannot be undertaken) put forward before recommending publication.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Threat of shock increases excitability and connectivity of the intraparietal sulcus" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by David Van Essen (Senior editor) and the Reviewing editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

I would like to thank the authors for their attempt at addressing my concerns. I'm pleased that the authors were able to spot errors in their pipeline (use of incorrect spatial filters) although it does appear that the major difference came from the down-sampling, as suggested in my previous review. Downsampling over such a small time window is obviously incorrect so these analyses should now be discarded.

Unfortunately, the adjacency matrices still don't look right – without seeing them plotted on a brain it's hard to judge exactly where the primary pathways of connectivity are (and I still can’t read the labels clearly in the pdf). As I have said previously, the highest connectivity in the α band should be in the occipital lobe whilst the highest connectivity in the β band should encompass bilateral parietal and occipital connections alongside tempero-parietal and fronto-parietal networks (again as in Hunt et al, 2016). In fact this does not seem to be the case. In what the authors have provided the α network looks like pure noise. There is clearly some structure to the β band connectivity matrix although this doesn't really look like one would expect. So I strongly suspect something is still wrong with the analysis.

Without looking at the data directly it’s hard for me to judge but I suspect that the problem is the short time windows (unless there are other more basic errors (similar to the incorrect spatial filter) which the authors have not discovered). It is known that a reasonable amount of data is required to make MEG connectivity analyses work reliably (Luizzi et al., Optimising experimental design for MEG resting state functional connectivity measurement, NeuroImage 2016) and perhaps this is the reason the adjacency matrices look so poor. In the light of these failed attempts, I suggest that a paragraph is added to the Discussion stating that MEG connectivity analysis would have been a useful means to probe these data; however the study design was poorly set up to make such analyses work.

Please note that this must now be your final attempt to satisfy the Board.

results.result: The threat of shock paradigm successfully induced elevated state anxiety in both MEG and fMRI experiments, as measured by subjective ratings of anxiety and fear, and by anxiety-potentiated startle in the MEG study. Anxiety and fear ratings were significantly higher during threat blocks compared to safe blocks in both experiments, with no significant differences between experiments. In the MEG study, startle magnitude was significantly greater during threat blocks, and anxiety ratings correlated significantly with startle magnitude across subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 provide converging evidence from multiple measures (subjective ratings and physiological startle response) across two independent experiments (MEG and fMRI) that the threat manipulation successfully induced anxiety. The statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests), sample sizes are adequate (N=28 MEG, N=25 fMRI), and p-values are highly significant (all p<0.001 except whole-brain GBC). The correlation between ratings and startle (C29, r=0.61, p=0.001) provides validation of the subjective measure. The lack of between-experiment differences (C27) supports consistency of the manipulation.

results.result: Threat of shock significantly increased whole-brain global brain connectivity (GBC) compared to safe conditions. Voxelwise analysis revealed three specific clusters showing increased GBC during threat: the right angular gyrus (largest cluster) and bilateral intraparietal sulcus (IPS). These effects remained significant after controlling for potential confounds including shock delivery, motion differences, and censoring.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 demonstrate robust increases in GBC during threat using appropriate statistical methods (paired t-tests with Monte Carlo cluster correction, alpha=0.05). The whole-brain effect (C31, t(24)=2.13, p=0.044) is modest but significant. The regional effects (C32-C33) are well-localized and the control analyses (C34) address important confounds including motion and shock-evoked activity, with all three regions remaining significant after these controls. The convergence of whole-brain and regional analyses strengthens the findings.

results.result: Threat increased functional connectivity between the bilateral IPS seed region and several regions of the frontoparietal attention network, including the thalamus, inferior parietal lobule, superior medial gyrus, precuneus, middle frontal gyrus, and angular gyrus.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by seed-based connectivity analysis using the IPS regions identified from the GBC analysis. The analysis used appropriate statistical methods (paired t-tests with cluster correction) and identified multiple regions consistent with the frontoparietal attention network. However, the authors acknowledge potential circularity in using GBC-identified regions as seeds, though they argue this approach limits interpretations to those supported by both analyses. The findings are consistent with the GBC results and provide anatomical specificity.

results.result: MEG recordings showed that alpha oscillations (~10 Hz) were a prominent feature of spontaneous neural activity. Threat significantly reduced alpha power compared to safe conditions in left parietal sensors and frontal sensors. Source localization revealed two clusters with reduced alpha power during threat: the left IPS (larger cluster) and mid-cingulate gyrus. The left IPS cluster from MEG substantially overlapped (46/81 voxels) with the left IPS cluster identified in the fMRI GBC analysis. These effects remained significant after controlling for differences in trial numbers between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 provide converging evidence from sensor-level and source-level MEG analyses that threat reduces alpha power in parietal regions. The identification of individual alpha frequency peaks (C39-C40) is methodologically sound. The sensor-level (C41-C42) and source-level (C43-C44) analyses used appropriate statistical methods (Monte Carlo cluster correction). The spatial overlap between MEG and fMRI findings (C45, 57% overlap) provides strong cross-modal validation. The control analysis (C46) addresses the confound of unequal trial numbers. The convergence of multiple analysis approaches and imaging modalities strongly supports these findings.

results.result: The intraparietal sulcus (IPS) shows both elevated neural activity (reduced alpha power indicating increased cortical excitability) and elevated global brain connectivity during threat. The IPS functions as a critical connectivity hub in the network mediating sustained state anxiety, with increased connectivity to regions important for attention control. Together, these findings suggest that threat of shock facilitates attentional processing through increased excitability and connectivity of the IPS.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C47, C48, C49, and C52 represent the primary integrative conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergent findings from fMRI (increased GBC and seed-based connectivity) and MEG (reduced alpha power) in the same anatomical region (IPS). The interpretation that reduced alpha reflects increased excitability (C48) is supported by established theory (C37) and citations. The characterization of IPS as a hub (C47, C52) is justified by the GBC findings and connectivity patterns. The inference that these changes facilitate attentional processing (C49) is reasonable given the known role of IPS in attention, though direct behavioral evidence is not provided in this study.

results.result: The IPS may contribute to hypervigilance in pathological anxiety. Enhanced attentional processing during threat may reflect hypervigilance, which could explain why threat facilitates performance on tasks requiring external attention focus but impairs performance on tasks requiring internal attention focus. Hyperactivation of the IPS during elevated state anxiety may account for these paradoxical performance effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C50, C51, C6, and C7 are explicitly speculative interpretations that extend beyond the current data. While the IPS findings are robust, the connection to hypervigilance (C5, C50) is inferential and not directly tested. The mechanistic explanations for differential effects on external vs. internal attention tasks (C51, C6, C7) are plausible hypotheses supported by citations to previous behavioral studies, but no behavioral data were collected in the current study to test these predictions. These remain reasonable but unvalidated hypotheses requiring future experimental work.

results.result: The increase in IPS connectivity (fMRI) and decrease in IPS alpha power (MEG) may reflect a common process of increased cortical excitability. Threat-induced alpha reduction may result from release of top-down inhibition, and may provide a mechanistic explanation for anxiety-potentiated startle by increasing cortical excitability. The decreases in alpha power may reflect greater perceptual sensitivity consistent with increased vigilance.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C62, C66, C67, and C74 integrate the fMRI and MEG findings with established theory about alpha oscillations. The inference that increased connectivity and decreased alpha reflect a common process (C60) is well-supported by the spatial overlap of findings and by previous literature showing negative correlations between alpha power and connectivity (C38, C55-C59). The mechanistic interpretations (C62, C66, C67, C74) are grounded in established theory about alpha function (C37, C61) and supported by appropriate citations. While these are interpretations rather than direct demonstrations, they are well-reasoned inferences from the data.

results.result: The reductions in alpha power were lateralized to the left hemisphere, resulting in a right-dominant parietal asymmetry. This pattern is consistent with theoretical models linking right-dominant parietal alpha to increased arousal, as threat of shock increases arousal and reduces left parietal alpha.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C80 describe an observed pattern in the data (left-lateralized alpha reduction) and connect it to theoretical models of alpha asymmetry and arousal (C79). The observation is clearly supported by the MEG results showing effects primarily in left parietal sensors and left IPS at the source level. The connection to arousal models (C80) is a reasonable inference supported by appropriate citations (C79), though the study did not independently measure arousal to test this interpretation directly. The finding is descriptive and the theoretical interpretation is plausible but not definitively tested.

results.result: A bias toward hyper-orienting during elevated state anxiety could explain conflicting findings about cognition-anxiety interactions. The authors hypothesize that threat-induced hyper-orienting improves sustained attention performance by reducing lapses, but impairs working memory performance by lowering the threshold for distractors to access working memory resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C84, and C85 are explicitly identified as speculative hypotheses. The authors acknowledge their results provide only indirect evidence for these ideas (C81). While the hypotheses are plausible and supported by citations to previous behavioral studies (C82, C83), no behavioral data were collected in the current study to test these predictions. These represent reasonable theoretical frameworks for future research but are not supported by the current experimental evidence.

results.result: Elevated anxiety in humans is primarily a cognitive state not fully captured by current translational models focused on the amygdala and fear circuitry. Because the most prominent region contributing to elevated state anxiety is cortical (IPS), it may be possible to target this region with neuromodulatory methods to reduce anxiety.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C89 represent broad interpretive conclusions and therapeutic implications. While the finding that IPS (a cortical attention region) rather than amygdala shows the most prominent changes is well-supported by the data, the conclusion that anxiety is 'primarily a cognitive state' (C88) overstates the findings. The study used unbiased whole-brain methods but did not directly compare effect sizes across all brain regions, and the absence of amygdala findings could reflect methodological factors (e.g., signal dropout in fMRI, limited MEG sensitivity to deep structures). The therapeutic speculation (C89) is reasonable but highly preliminary, requiring substantial additional research to validate.

results.result: Enhanced GBC in the angular gyrus may reflect heightened awareness of the current context, though this is acknowledged as a post hoc explanation requiring future investigation.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is explicitly identified by the authors as a post hoc speculative hypothesis. While the finding of increased GBC in the right angular gyrus is supported by the data (C32), the functional interpretation is uncertain.
